time_scope: NIKL 1991 normative list versus Choi 2001 spoken survey
claim: Word-medial English /l/ is overwhelmingly adapted as geminate [ll] in Present Day Korean, but spoken data contain substantially more singleton [ɾ] than the normative written list: NIKL has 2.3% singleton (7/308), whereas Choi's 367-speaker survey has 9.1% singleton tokens (335/3670) across seven intervocalic and three obstruent+/l/ loanwords.
normalized_environment: LOAN_MEDIAL_L has VARIABLE SINGLETON vs GEMINATE adaptation; spoken singleton > normative written singleton
exceptions_or_counterexamples: NIKL is explicitly described as normative and therefore not a reliable estimate of spoken variability; Choi's ten target words are too few for definitive word-level generalization.

time_scope: Enlightenment Period Korean 1880-1910 and 1930s written corpora
claim: Singleton adaptation/transcription of medial /l/ is less frequent in obstruent+/l/ clusters than intervocalically in both historical corpora: EPK 15.2% in clusters vs 19.6% intervocalically; 1930s 32.3% vs 40.1%. This direction recurs after regression control and therefore cannot be treated as a single lexical accident.
formal_environment: English /l/ in V_V versus obstruent+l cluster
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Rates are raw historical written proportions and are potentially confounded by spelling and Japanese mediation; controlled models are recorded separately.

time_scope: J.-K. Lee 1937 corpus as analyzed by Kang 2012
claim: Japanese mediation is the strongest measured predictor of singleton medial-/l/ adaptation in the 1930s corpus. Raw singleton rates are 94.9% in items coded with Japanese influence versus 31.9% with no Japanese influence and 35.9% in uncoded items; in the logistic model the Japanese-influence coefficient is about +3.57.
formal_environment: MEDIAL English /l/ in loans, conditioned by borrowing channel
normalized_environment: JAPANESE_MEDIATION strongly favors SINGLETON liquid adaptation
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Coding Japanese influence is conservative: some items coded as lacking the diagnostic trait may still contain other Japanese-mediated properties.

time_scope: J.-K. Lee 1937 corpus as analyzed by Kang 2012
claim: After controlling competing factors in the 1930s medial-/l/ data, singleton adaptation is disfavored when English /l/ is in an obstruent cluster, post-tonic, or associated with the English initial syllable. The retained coefficients are cluster -0.51029, post-tonic -0.36997, and InitialE -0.32529, all significant; Japanese mediation remains much larger in magnitude.
formal_environment: MEDIAL English /l/ -> singleton versus geminate, conditioned by cluster/prosodic position
normalized_environment: CLUSTER + POSTTONIC + ENGLISH_INITIAL_SYLLABLE favor GEMINATE relative to SINGLETON
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Kang treats liquid-duration sensitivity as a small effect relative to Japanese mediation and cluster-related pressure; the analysis is probabilistic, not a categorical phonotactic ban.

time_scope: EPK through 1930s to Present Day Korean
claim: The recurrent cluster effect runs opposite to a simple input-duration account: singleton medial-/l/ is lower in clusters, where English liquids are expected to be shorter. Kang argues that gemination shortens the preceding epenthetic vowel, so a preference for a short, nonprominent epenthetic vowel can override faithfulness to input liquid duration.

source_forms.reported_controlled_difference: estimated singleton rate lower in clusters than intervocalic position by 8.2% in the 1930s model
source_forms.repair_comparison: cluster adaptation with epenthetic vowel: geminate [ɨl.lV] versus singleton [ɨ.ɾV]

formal_environment: OBSTRUENT+L source cluster -> V-epenthesis + singleton/geminate liquid
normalized_environment: EPENTHETIC_VOWEL prosody interacts with LIQUID quantity; GEMINATE favored in clusters
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Input duration still has a smaller independent effect in post-tonic/initial-syllable conditions; this is not a claim that duration is irrelevant.
